options: Define which issue categories to report and which to skip, with an example of each.
Turn off the noisiest category for now while its criteria are rewritten.
Require each finding to cite the exact line and state its concrete impact.
Add severity levels, with a written criterion for each level.

h.stem: Developers now ignore every review comment because the “naming” category is wrong most of the time. The other categories are accurate. What's the best immediate step?
why: Right when the reviewer reports things the team doesn't want at all. Here one category is unreliable.
Removing the unreliable category restores trust in the accurate ones while its criteria are fixed.
Right when findings are vague. These are specific, just wrong.
Right when urgent and minor findings look alike. Here one category is wrong.

p.stem: The reviewer reports style nits, possible bugs and security holes with the same urgency. Developers can't tell what must be fixed before merging. What's the best step?
why: Right when unwanted categories are reported. All of these are wanted; their priority is unclear.
Right when one category is unreliable. Here they all lack priority.
Right when findings are vague. Here they're specific but unranked.
Defined severity levels let developers see what blocks a merge.

options: Define exactly what counts as a “termination clause,” with included and excluded examples.
Make the field nullable, and return null when the document doesn't contain one.
Add a field where the model explains how it arrived at each value.
Require a page and section reference for every extracted value.

h.stem: The extractor labels auto-renewal and notice-period clauses as “termination clauses.” The legal team means only clauses that allow early exit. What fixes this?
why: Explicit criteria with edge examples tell the model where the category's boundary is.
Right when values are invented for absent fields. Here a real clause is mislabeled.
Right when you need to audit reasoning. It won't change where the boundary is.
Right when reviewers can't find the source. Here the category itself is misunderstood.

p.stem: Reviewers can't check extracted values quickly: they have to search 80-page contracts for where each one came from. What fixes this?
why: Right when a category is misunderstood. Here the values are fine but hard to verify.
Right when values are invented for absent fields. Here the issue is verification time.
Explaining the derivation doesn't say where in the document to look.
A location for every value lets reviewers jump straight to the evidence.

options: Review each file separately, then do one pass on cross-file interactions.
Have a second, independent instance review without the first one's reasoning.
Have the reviewer give a confidence for each finding to direct human attention.
Review the whole diff in a single pass, with the PR description as context.

h.stem: Human reviewers spend equal time on all 40 findings per PR, though a handful are far shakier than the rest. The team wants human time spent where it matters most. What fits best?
why: Right when attention spreads thin over many files. Here the findings already exist.
Right when a reviewer checks its own work. Here the issue is where humans spend time.
Per-finding confidence lets humans check the uncertain findings first.
Right for small diffs. It doesn't rank the findings.

p.stem: Claude reviews the code it just generated, in the same conversation, and approves nearly everything. What fits best?
why: Right for large diffs. The issue here is self-review.
An instance without the generator's reasoning doesn't share its blind spots.
Right for directing human attention. The reviewer still shares the author's blind spots.
Right for small diffs. Self-review would remain.

options: Have a second instance, without the first one's reasoning, re-extract a sample to compare.
Have the model report confidence per field and send low-confidence fields to people.
Check that the totals add up, and retry with the error when they don't.
Split long documents into sections, extract from each, then merge the results.

h.stem: Extraction from 60-page contracts misses clauses that appear late in the document. Short contracts are extracted accurately. What fits best?
why: Right when an extractor confirms its own errors. Here attention fades over a long document.
Right for directing human review. The missed clauses would still be missed.
Right for values a rule can check. Missing clauses aren't caught by arithmetic.
Smaller passes keep attention on each section, and a merge step combines them.

p.stem: The same instance that extracted the data is asked to verify it, and it confirms its own errors. What fits best?
why: An independent instance doesn't share the first one's reasoning, so it can catch its errors.
Right for prioritizing human review. Self-verification would still miss these errors.
Right for checkable arithmetic. Most fields can't be checked that way.
Right for long documents. The problem here is self-verification.

options: Add two or three borderline findings as examples, with the reasoning for each.
Write explicit criteria for which categories to report and which to skip.
Show an example of the exact output structure for one finding.
Add examples from each of the languages the reviewer covers.

h.stem: The reviewer handles clear-cut issues well but is inconsistent on borderline ones, such as whether an unchecked error in a test helper matters. What works best?
why: Examples of the hard cases, with the reasoning, show how to judge the borderline.
Right when whole categories are unwanted. Here the problem is borderline judgment within one.
Right when the format varies. Here the judgment varies.
Right when quality differs by language. Here it differs by how clear-cut the case is.

p.stem: Review findings come back in a different shape each run: sometimes a list, sometimes prose, sometimes a table. What works best?
why: Right for borderline judgment. Here the content is fine; the shape varies.
Right when unwanted categories appear. Here the shape varies.
An example of the exact format shows the model what to reproduce every time.
Right when quality differs by language. Here the shape varies.

options: Add example documents in each layout, showing where each field is found.
Add an example of a document missing a field, with null as the output.
Add an example that shows the reasoning for an ambiguous date.
Define each field precisely in the prompt, with its expected format.

h.stem: One European supplier writes dates like 03/04/25, and the extractor reads them sometimes day-first and sometimes month-first. What works best?
why: Right when layouts vary. Here one format is ambiguous.
Right when values are invented for missing fields. The date here is present.
Showing the reasoning (European supplier, so day first) teaches the model how to resolve the ambiguity.
Right when the field's meaning is unclear. Here the format is known but read inconsistently.

p.stem: Extraction works on the standard invoice template but fails on invoices that put the total in a footer table or a sidebar. What works best?
why: Examples of each layout show the model where fields live when the structure changes.
Right when fields are absent. Here they're present in other places.
Right for ambiguous values. Here the problem is location.
Right when a field's meaning is unclear. Here its location varies.

options: Set tool_choice to "any" so a tool call is required.
Force one tool with tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": …}.
Make the fields that may be absent nullable in the schema.
Add an "other" enum value plus a free-text detail field.

h.stem: The document type isn't known in advance, and there's one extraction tool per type. Sometimes the model replies in plain text instead of calling any of them. What fixes this?
why: Requiring some tool call guarantees structured output while letting the model pick the right schema. (Exam framing; see Exam vs. today for current model support.)
Right when one specific tool must run. Here the right tool depends on the document.
Right when values are invented for absent fields. Here no tool is called.
Right when real values fall outside the categories. Here no tool is called.

p.stem: Every document must go through extract_metadata before any other processing. The model sometimes calls a different tool first. What fixes this?
why: Right when any of several tools is acceptable. Here one specific tool must run first.
Forcing the named tool guarantees it runs first. (Exam framing; see Exam vs. today for current model support.)
Right when values are invented. Here the wrong tool runs.
Right when categories don't fit. Here the wrong tool runs.

options: Make the fields that may be absent nullable in the schema.
Add an "other" enum value with a free-text detail field.
Define the output with a strict JSON schema in the tool definition.
Add a validation step that checks the values against business rules.

h.stem: Some contracts have no renewal date. In those cases the extractor fills in a plausible-looking date anyway. What fixes this?
why: If the schema requires a value, the model invents one; nullable lets it say “absent.”
Right when real values fall outside the categories. Here there's no value at all.
Right for syntax errors. The output here is valid but invented.
Right for checkable rules. A plausible invented date passes most of them.

p.stem: The payment_terms enum has four values, but about 8% of contracts use other terms, and the model forces them into the nearest value. What fixes this?
why: Right when a value is absent. Here a real value doesn't fit the list.
An escape value plus detail captures real cases that the list doesn't cover.
Right for syntax errors. The output is valid, just forced into the wrong category.
Right for checkable rules. A wrong but valid category passes them.

options: Retry, including the specific validation error in the follow-up request.
Stop retrying and send the document to human review.
Extract both the stated total and a calculated total, and flag mismatches.
Record a detected_pattern with each flag to see which ones reviewers dismiss.

h.stem: Validation fails because tax_id is empty. Checking the source PDF shows the document never contains a tax ID, and two retries made no difference. What's the right next step?
why: Right when the value exists but came back in the wrong form. Retries can't find information that isn't there.
When the information is missing from the source, a person must resolve it.
Right for checking internal consistency. The problem here is a missing value.
Right for learning from reviewer dismissals. This is a single missing value.

p.stem: About 5% of extractions fail validation because dates come back as “March 3rd” instead of ISO 8601. The dates are in the documents. What's the right next step?
why: The value exists; telling the model exactly what failed lets it correct the format.
Right when the source lacks the value. Here it's present.
Right for internal consistency. This is a format error.
Right for analyzing reviewer dismissals. This is a format error.

options: Retry with the validation error and the original document in the follow-up.
Extract the line items, the stated total and a calculated total, then compare them.
Make the field nullable so the model can report that a value is absent.
Record a detected_pattern with each flag to see which ones reviewers dismiss.

h.stem: Totals taken from the invoice summary box sometimes don't match the line items. Nobody notices until finance reconciles at month end. What fits best?
why: Right when a known error needs correcting. Here nothing detects the error.
Extracting both totals lets the pipeline catch inconsistencies on its own.
Right when values are absent. Here they're present but inconsistent.
Right for analyzing dismissals. Here the error goes unnoticed.

p.stem: Reviewers dismiss many of the extractor's “anomaly” flags. The team wants to learn which kinds of flag to stop raising. What fits best?
why: Right for correcting format errors. This is about which flags are useful.
Right for detecting inconsistencies. This is about which flags are useful.
Right when values are absent. This is about which flags are useful.
Tagging each flag with its pattern shows which patterns reviewers dismiss.

options: Use the Message Batches API for the nightly audit of every repository.
Keep synchronous calls for the pre-merge check that developers wait on.
Refine the prompt on a sample first, then submit the full batch.
Resubmit only the failed requests, matched by their custom_id.

h.stem: The team moved the pre-merge check to the Message Batches API to save 50%. Developers now wait hours for results before they can merge. What fits best?
why: Right for non-blocking work like nightly audits. A pre-merge check is blocking.
Batches can take up to 24 hours; a check people wait on needs a synchronous response.
Right before the first large run. The problem here is latency.
Right after a batch with failures. The problem here is latency.

p.stem: A weekly scan of 2,000 repositories runs through synchronous calls. Nobody needs the results before Monday morning, and cost is the main complaint. What fits best?
why: Non-urgent bulk work suits batches, which cost 50% less.
Right for blocking checks. Nobody waits on this one.
Right for a new prompt. This scan's prompt is established.
Right after failures. Here the issue is cost.

options: Submit all 50,000 documents through the Message Batches API.
Resubmit only the failed documents, matched by their custom_id.
Run the prompt on a sample of a few hundred, refine it, then batch the rest.
Process documents synchronously as they arrive.

h.stem: A 50,000-document batch has finished: 600 requests errored and the rest succeeded. The team plans to rerun all 50,000. What fits best?
why: That reprocesses 49,400 documents that already succeeded.
Rerun only what failed; custom_id ties each result to its document.
Right for an untested prompt. This one has already run.
Right when results are needed immediately. This is a bulk rerun.

p.stem: A new extraction prompt has never run on real documents. The team must process 50,000 by Friday at the lowest cost. What fits best?
why: Batching an untested prompt risks paying for 50,000 bad results.
Right after a batch with failures. Nothing has run yet.
Fix problems on a sample cheaply first, then batch the rest at the lower price.
Right when results are needed immediately. It costs more and nothing here is urgent.
